overview.title: Finding the right model size: the IMDb reference model
overview.main_topic: Choosing model size empirically on the validation set, and the 16-16-1 IMDb model used as the baseline for the regularization experiments
overview.central_idea: No formula gives you the right number of layers or units. You find it by experiment: start small and grow the model until validation loss stops improving much. The condensed chapter 4 IMDb model (listing 5.10) is the reference that the smaller model (listing 5.11, starting here) and later variants are compared against.
overview.importance: This page sets up the controlled experiment that runs through the rest of section 5.4.4. Every later curve (figures 5.18, 5.19, 5.20, 5.22) compares a variant against `history_original` from listing 5.10, so you need to understand exactly what that baseline is.

summary:
This page continues the subsubsection **Reducing the network's size** (started on p.185). The authors first point out a hard fact: there is **no magical formula** for the right number of layers or the right size for each layer. You have to evaluate several architectures, and you do it **on the validation set, not on the test set**, because the test set must stay untouched for the final unbiased evaluation (see p.135 and p.173). They recommend a concrete search procedure: **start with relatively few layers and parameters, then increase layer size or add layers until validation loss shows diminishing returns.**

To make this concrete, they bring back the movie-review classifier from chapter 4 in condensed form as **Listing 5.10, "Original model"**. It loads IMDb with the 10,000 most frequent words, multi-hot encodes every review into a 10,000-dimensional 0/1 vector with `vectorize_sequences`, and builds a `keras.Sequential` model with two `Dense(16, activation="relu")` layers and a `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")` output. It compiles the model with `rmsprop`, `binary_crossentropy` and accuracy, then trains it for 20 epochs with batch size 512, keeping 40% of the training data for validation (`validation_split=0.4`). The returned `History` object is kept as `history_original` so its validation loss curve can serve as the **reference** in the comparisons that follow.

The page ends with the start of **Listing 5.11, "Version of the model with lower capacity"**, where the first hidden layer has only **4 units** instead of 16. The listing continues on p.187, where the second hidden layer also has 4 units and the compile/fit settings are identical, so the only variable is capacity. Figure 5.18 on p.187 then compares the two validation-loss curves.

paragraphs.excerpt: Unfortunately, there is no magical formula to determine the right number of layers
paragraphs.what_it_says: There is no formula that gives the right depth or width. You must try several architectures, evaluating them on the validation set (never the test set), and the usual procedure is to start small and grow the layers, or add layers, until validation loss stops improving much.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Model size is a hyperparameter, and you pick it by search. Because you are choosing it from validation results, the validation set becomes part of the model-selection process. That is exactly why the test set has to stay out of the loop. 'Diminishing returns' means you stop when one more increase in capacity buys only a tiny improvement in validation loss, or makes it worse.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This turns the abstract trade-off from p.185 (too much capacity overfits, too little underfits) into a practical recipe you can apply to any new problem. The same procedure shows up again in the universal workflow (p.207: 'Try different architectures; add or remove layers').
paragraphs.technical_idea: Searching over capacity on held-out data approximates the bias-variance trade-off empirically. Growing from small to large is cheap at first and reveals the capacity at which validation loss bottoms out.

terminology.meaning: Number of learnable parameters, determined by the number of layers and units per layer (p.185).
Each further increase in size gives a smaller, eventually negligible or negative, improvement in validation loss.

connections: p.185: model size is defined as the number of learnable parameters; too small underfits, too large memorizes
p.135: why the test set must not be used for tuning choices such as model size
p.181: the opposite direction, making a model bigger when it cannot overfit

concepts.name: Model capacity (model size)
concepts.definition: How much information a model can store: its number of learnable parameters, set by the number of layers and units per layer.
concepts.intuition: Capacity is the model's 'memory budget'. With a big budget it can memorize the training set. With a small one it has to compress, keeping only patterns that predict the target.
concepts.technical: For a Dense stack, parameters = sum over layers of (inputs x units + units). The reference IMDb model has 10000x16+16 + 16x16+16 + 16x1+1 = 160,305 parameters.
concepts.significance: Capacity is the first regularization knob in 5.4.4. Reducing it is the simplest way to fight overfitting.
concepts.example: Shrinking the hidden layers from 16 to 4 units (listing 5.11) cuts parameters from about 160K to about 40K.
concepts.misconception: More capacity does not always mean better results. Beyond a certain point it only speeds up memorization and makes overfitting worse (figure 5.19, p.188).

concepts.name: Validation set for architecture search
concepts.definition: Held-out data used to compare candidate models and hyperparameters, such as layer sizes.
concepts.intuition: It is the practice exam you use to decide how to study. The test set is the real exam, which you take only once.
concepts.technical: Here the validation data is created by `validation_split=0.4`, which holds out the last 40% of the training arrays (10,000 of the 25,000 reviews) and reports `val_loss` and `val_accuracy` after every epoch.
concepts.significance: Choosing the architecture from validation scores leaks information into the model, so the test set must stay separate (p.135, p.173).
concepts.example: You compare the val_loss curves of the 16-unit and 4-unit models and keep the size that reaches the lowest val_loss.
concepts.misconception: Using the test set to choose layer sizes makes the test score optimistically biased.

concepts.name: Regularization by reducing size
concepts.definition: Techniques that keep the model from fitting the training data perfectly, in order to improve validation performance (p.185). Reducing network size is the first such technique.
concepts.intuition: A smaller model cannot memorize, so it is forced to generalize.
concepts.technical: Lowering the parameter count restricts the hypothesis space, which lowers variance at the cost of some bias.
concepts.significance: This frames the experiments on p.186-188 as a regularization study.
concepts.misconception: Regularization does not mean 'making the model worse'. It trades training fit for better generalization.

concepts.name: Multi-hot encoding (vectorize_sequences)
concepts.definition: Turning a list of word indices into a fixed-length 0/1 vector with 1s at the indices that occur.
concepts.intuition: A checklist of 10,000 words: tick every word that appears in the review.
concepts.technical: `results[i, sequence] = 1.0` uses NumPy integer-array indexing to set every listed column of row i at once.
concepts.significance: It is the input representation of the reference model, giving an input dimension of 10,000.
concepts.example: A review with word indices [3, 7, 7] becomes a vector with 1.0 at positions 3 and 7. The repeat is ignored.
concepts.misconception: Multi-hot vectors do not record word order or word counts.

code.title: Original model
code.original_code:
from keras.datasets import imdb

(train_data, train_labels), _ = imdb.load_data(num_words=10000)

def vectorize_sequences(sequences, dimension=10000):
    results = np.zeros((len(sequences), dimension))
    for i, sequence in enumerate(sequences):
        results[i, sequence] = 1.0
    return results

train_data = vectorize_sequences(train_data)

model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        layers.Dense(16, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(16, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"),
    ]
)
model.compile(
    optimizer="rmsprop",
    loss="binary_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
history_original = model.fit(
    train_data,
    train_labels,
    epochs=20,
    batch_size=512,
    validation_split=0.4,
)
code.what_it_does: Loads the IMDb training reviews, multi-hot encodes them into 10,000-dimensional vectors, builds and compiles the 16-16-1 binary classifier from chapter 4, and trains it for 20 epochs with 40% of the data held out for validation. It stores the training history as `history_original` for later comparison.

line_explanations.explanation: Imports the IMDb loader and loads only the 10,000 most frequent words. The test split is discarded with `_` because this experiment only uses training plus validation data.
`vectorize_sequences` allocates a zero matrix of shape (num_reviews, 10000) and sets to 1.0 the columns listed in each review (multi-hot encoding, as in listing 4.3, p.132).
Replaces `train_data` (lists of ints) with the float matrix of shape (25000, 10000).
The reference architecture: two hidden Dense layers of 16 relu units and one sigmoid output unit that gives the probability that the review is positive.
Compiles with the RMSprop optimizer, binary crossentropy loss (suited to a sigmoid output) and accuracy as the metric.
Trains for 20 epochs in mini-batches of 512. `validation_split=0.4` holds out the last 40% of the samples, so val_loss is reported each epoch. The returned History is kept as `history_original`.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: 25,000 reviews as (25000, 10000) float vectors with labels 0/1. Output: a trained model plus `history_original.history`, a dict with 'loss', 'accuracy', 'val_loss' and 'val_accuracy', each a list of 20 per-epoch values.
code.algorithm: Mini-batch gradient descent (RMSprop) on binary crossentropy, evaluating on a fixed held-out split after every epoch.
code.theory_link: This is the baseline for the capacity experiment. Its validation loss is minimal around epoch 4 and then rises (figure 5.18, p.187), which is classic overfitting.

parameters.name: num_words=10000
parameters.role: Vocabulary size, which also sets the input dimension.

parameters.name: Dense(16)
parameters.role: Width of each hidden layer. This is the capacity knob varied on p.186-188.

parameters.name: epochs=20
parameters.role: Deliberately long, so the overfitting phase is visible.

parameters.name: batch_size=512
parameters.role: Samples per gradient update. About 30 updates per epoch on 15,000 training samples.

parameters.name: validation_split=0.4
parameters.role: Fraction of the data held out for validation (10,000 reviews).

pitfalls: The listing assumes `import numpy as np`, `import keras` and `from keras import layers` were run earlier. They are not shown in this condensed listing.
`validation_split` takes the *last* 40% of the arrays before any shuffling. That is fine for IMDb, which is pre-shuffled, but not for data sorted by class.
Re-running `model = keras.Sequential(...)` creates a fresh model. Calling `fit` again on the same model object would continue training instead.

deeper.title: Parameter counts of the models compared in 5.4.4
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, here is the arithmetic. With a 10,000-dimensional input, a Dense layer has `inputs*units + units` parameters.

| model | layer 1 | layer 2 | output | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16-16-1 (listing 5.10) | 160,016 | 272 | 17 | **160,305** |
| 4-4-1 (listing 5.11) | 40,004 | 20 | 5 | **40,029** |
| 512-512-1 (listing 5.12, p.187) | 5,120,512 | 262,656 | 513 | **5,383,681** |

Almost all the parameters sit in the first layer, because it touches all 10,000 input dimensions. That is why width matters so much here.

deeper.title: The size-search loop as a procedure
deeper.body:
1. Start with a small model (few layers, few units).
2. Train it with a validation split and record the minimum val_loss.
3. Increase width or add a layer and repeat.
4. Stop when the minimum val_loss improves only marginally, or starts getting worse.
5. Only then evaluate the chosen model on the test set.

Steps 1-4 restate the book's paragraph. Step 5 follows from its insistence on using the validation set, not the test set.

deeper.title: Why a controlled comparison
deeper.body: Listings 5.10 and 5.11 share data, optimizer, loss, epochs, batch size and validation split. Only layer width differs, so any change in the val_loss curve (figure 5.18) can be blamed on capacity. Note (not in the book): single runs are noisy because initialization and batching are random. In serious work you would repeat each configuration with several seeds.

misconceptions.claim: There is a rule of thumb that gives the right number of layers and units.
misconceptions.correction: The book says plainly that there is no magical formula. Size is found by evaluating architectures on validation data.

misconceptions.claim: It is fine to compare architectures on the test set as long as you do it only a few times.
misconceptions.correction: Any model choice made from test results leaks test information. Compare on validation data and keep the test set for the final evaluation.

misconceptions.claim: The best search strategy is to start with a huge model and shrink it.
misconceptions.correction: The book recommends starting with relatively few layers and parameters and growing until validation loss shows diminishing returns.

takeaways: No formula gives the right model size. Find it by experiment on the validation set, never the test set.
Start with few layers and parameters, then grow until validation loss shows diminishing returns.
Listing 5.10 is the reference model: 16-16-1 Dense layers on 10,000-dimensional multi-hot input, rmsprop, binary crossentropy, 20 epochs, batch 512, validation_split=0.4.
Its history is stored as history_original so later variants can be compared against it.

questions.question: According to the page, how should you determine the right number of layers and layer sizes?
options: Use a formula based on the number of training samples
Evaluate different architectures on the validation set, starting small and growing until validation loss shows diminishing returns
Evaluate different architectures on the test set and keep the best
Always use the largest model your hardware allows
questions.answer: Evaluate different architectures on the validation set, starting small and growing until validation loss shows diminishing returns
questions.explanation: The book says there is no magical formula (so the first option is wrong) and insists on the validation set, not the test set (so the third is wrong). The largest model overfits badly (p.188), which rules out the fourth.

questions.question: What does validation_split=0.4 do in listing 5.10, and how many reviews end up in validation?
questions.answer: It holds out the last 40% of the training arrays as validation data, evaluated after every epoch. That is 10,000 of the 25,000 reviews, leaving 15,000 for training.
questions.explanation: Keras slices off the final fraction of x and y before training and reports val_loss and val_accuracy for it each epoch.

questions.question: Compute the number of trainable parameters of the reference model (input 10,000, Dense 16, Dense 16, Dense 1).
Why does listing 5.11 keep the optimizer, loss, epochs, batch size and validation split identical to listing 5.10?
questions.answer: To make it a controlled experiment. Only capacity (layer width) changes, so differences in the validation curves can be attributed to model size.
questions.explanation: If several settings changed at once, figure 5.18 could not tell you which one caused the different overfitting behaviour.

questions.question: What does the line results[i, sequence] = 1.0 do inside vectorize_sequences?
questions.answer: It sets to 1.0, in row i, every column whose index appears in the list `sequence`. This is multi-hot encoding through NumPy integer-array indexing.
questions.explanation: `sequence` is a list of word indices, so indexing with it addresses all those positions at once. Repeated indices are simply set to 1 again.

questions.question: Could you explain to a colleague why the test set must not be used to choose model size, and describe the procedure the book recommends instead?
questions.answer: Self-check: choosing on the test set leaks information and biases the final score. Instead, compare sizes on validation data, growing from small until validation loss has diminishing returns.
questions.explanation: See the first paragraph of the page and p.135.
